title: Shoftim: the nearest town (Deuteronomy 21:1–9)
hookLine: for an unsolved death, the nearest town's elders declare their hands did not shed this blood

lines: A BODY IN AN OPEN FIELD.
cards: A body is found in an open field, between towns. Nobody saw what happened. There's no suspect, no witness, no trail.
A case like that can quietly go cold: a file in a drawer, a name nobody says again. The Torah won't let it go cold.

It sends out the elders and judges with measuring lines, to find out one thing: which town is closest to where the body lies. And then that town, which did nothing wrong as far as anyone knows, has to answer.

teach.b: The ritual is ancient and stark. The elders of the nearest town take a young heifer that has never worked down to a valley with flowing water, and the rite is performed there.

teach.h: OUR HANDS HAVE NOT SHED THIS BLOOD.
teach.b: Then the elders wash their hands over it and say, in the old Jewish translation: "Our hands have not shed this blood, neither have our eyes seen it."
It's called the eglah arufah, the heifer whose neck is broken, and the rabbis stopped at the elders' words.
The Mishnah, in tractate Sotah, asks: would it ever cross anyone's mind that the elders of the court are murderers? So what are they really saying?

teach.h: WE DIDN'T SEND HIM AWAY HUNGRY.
teach.b: The Mishnah's answer: he didn't come to us and we send him away without food. We didn't see him and let him go on alone, without someone to walk with him.
The elders are declaring that their town didn't fail him in the small ways. No one turned him away hungry. No one let a stranger walk out onto a dangerous road unescorted.

From this the rabbis drew a duty called levayah, accompanying a guest part of the way when they leave. So the strange ritual makes an ordinary point. A death on the road isn't only the killer's business.
It's a question for the nearest town: did we feed him? Did we walk with him?

how: The heifer rite hasn't been performed for many centuries, but Jewish law still teaches levayah, accompanying a departing guest some distance, which the rabbis drew from the elders' declaration.

o: elders, the leaders of the town nearest the body
judges, the ones sent out to measure the field
witnesses, the ones who testify in a murder case

games.q: inside the nearest town — tap the pairs.
p: the heifer whose neck is broken
our hands have not shed this blood

s: the Mishnah says the elders are suspected of murder
it asks if anyone would think that, and says no: they declare they didn't send him off hungry or alone.
the rabbis drew a duty to accompany guests from this passage
levayah: walk your guest part of the way.
the closest town has to answer even though no one there is accused
that's the point: the nearest town answers.

games.q: you're an elder of the nearest town. you didn't know the man, and you didn't harm him. what does the Mishnah say your declaration really means?
o: we have no connection to this.
we didn't send him away hungry or let him walk alone.
games.why: Mishnah Sotah: he didn't come to us and leave without food; we didn't see him and let him go without escort.

practice: Picture the few blocks around where you live: the badly lit corner, the neighbor who hasn't been seen in a while, the person who sleeps in the doorway by the store, the kid who walks home alone.
You didn't cause any of it, but you're the nearest town. Hold one of them in mind and ask the Mishnah's two questions: is anyone going hungry here, and is anyone walking alone?

wordCard.voice: Shoftim. Judges. The portion that ends with elders measuring to the nearest town, and that town answering.

orig.note: Hebrew: the heifer whose neck is broken. the rite for an unsolved killing in Deuteronomy 21.

carryVoice: Your line: the nearest town answers. Even when it did nothing wrong. That's day five hundred six.
